title: Super Micro's Margin Surprise Is Already Guided Back Down
detail:
Super Micro's Margin Surprise Is Already Guided Back Down
Trefis Team
Fri, August 14, 2026 at 7:38 AM PDT 3 min read
SMCI
^GSPC
ANET
DELL
NTAP
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

The mix that produced it included contracts pushed out of the June quarter, and the September guide already takes the margin back down.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) reported its June quarter after the close on August 11, and the stock rose 19% the next trading day, against 0.3% for the S&P 500. The market bought a profit number and a guide, not the revenue the quarter delivered, and management has already said why that profit number does not repeat.

Why A 17.6% Gross Margin Arrived With Revenue At The Low End

Adjusted earnings were $1.70 a share against the 92 cents analysts expected, while revenue fell slightly short of their forecast. The beat sits in gross margin, 17.6% on a non-GAAP basis against the company's own guidance of 8.2% to 8.4%, and the CFO named that margin the primary reason the results exceeded guidance.

That margin came out of what did not ship. Revenue of $11.1 billion, up 93% year over year, landed near the low end of an $11 billion to $12.5 billion guide, which the CFO put down to delays in customer readiness. Those delays reshaped the mix: OEM appliance and large data center revenue fell 26% sequentially, taking its share of the quarter from 72% to 50%, while enterprise and channel revenue nearly doubled sequentially to take the other half.

High-volume GPU work carries a much lower margin than the CPU, storage, and enterprise lines, by the CEO's own account, so the quarter the large data center work slid out of is the quarter the margin rose. Gross margin in the prior quarter was 10.1%, and the CFO put roughly 75% of the 750-basis-point sequential improvement on better customer and product mix, including contracts deferred out of the June quarter. The rest came from lower tariff costs and an inventory reserve benefit the CFO called nonrecurring.

The Guide Brings The Volume Back, And The Old Margin With It

For the September quarter the company guided revenue to $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion and gross margin back to 10.4% to 10.8%, with the CFO placing the deferred contracts there and perhaps beyond. That guide is management's own statement that 17.6% is not the run rate: the volume comes back and margin goes back to where fiscal 2026 ran as a whole, 10.9%. Margins that hold up rather than spike are one thing the businesses inside the Trefis High Quality Portfolio have in common.

Conversion, Not Demand, Decides Fiscal 2027

Demand is not the open question. Over $60 billion of new orders landed in the June quarter alone, against $39.1 billion of revenue for all of fiscal 2026, the year that quarter closed out. The company expects to fulfill those orders over the coming quarters, behind a fiscal 2027 revenue target of $65 billion to $72 billion. Capacity is not the constraint either, with manufacturing on track to exceed 6,000 racks a month, more than 3,000 of them direct liquid-cooled racks. Conversion is, and the constraints the CEO named sat on the customer's side: power, cooling and networking. The higher-margin work is the enterprise CPU-based server, storage, and IoT product lines built out since early 2026, and those have to keep growing once the large racks return. The test is September-quarter revenue against that guide, and whether margin holds the 10.4% to 10.8% guided with it, the question a guidance-driven momentum screen exists to answer.

Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) was one of the most shorted stocks by hedge funds in the first half of 2026, according to the Data Insights Crowding Report.

This meant that a lot of investors were betting that the shares will fall. Only two companies were more heavily shorted, Data Insights found: Charter Communications (NASDAQ: CHTR) and Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ: SMCI).

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

It has been a wild 12 months for Oracle stock. It spiked to an all-time high last summer on strong earnings and a growing backlog. As of June, the end of its fiscal year, it had amassed a huge order backlog, with a whopping $638 billion in remaining performance obligations.

Image source: Getty Images.

The backlog was highlighted by a $300 billion deal with OpenAI for cloud computing.

But it also has infrastructure deals with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), AMD (NASDAQ: AMD), and Meta (NASDAQ: META), to name just some of the major partnerships.

Oracle stock soared to an all-time closing high of $324 on Sept. 10, 2025. It's now trading at about $153 per share, after losing more than half its value. What happened?

Shorting Oracle

A confluence of factors are responsible.

The major factor is the huge capital spending plans to build out data centers and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure to fulfill these contracts. Oracle reported $21 billion in capital expenditures (capex) last year and a whopping $55 billion in fiscal 2026. This left Oracle with negative cash flow of $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026.

And in fiscal 2027, the company plans to raise another $40 billion through debt and equity financing to fund its capex.

Its debt is through the roof at $167 billion and a sky-high 388% debt-to-equity ratio.

Investors also are concerned about OpenAI's finances and whether it can fulfill all its contracts, including those with Oracle. It certainly plays into the growing investor narrative that AI stocks are spending too much on infrastructure in relation to the potential return.

Is Oracle stock a buy now?

So, with a series of setbacks, not to mention a high valuation, it is clear to see why investors have been betting on Oracle's stock to drop.

However, after such a steep drop, the share valuation has returned to a reasonable level. Oracle stock has a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 25, a forward P/E of 18, and a low five-year price/earnings-to-growth ratio, or PEG ratio, of 0.85. A PEG of less than 1 indicates that the stock is undervalued relative to its anticipated earnings expectations.

Expanding AI inference workloads are projected to expand the enterprise data center flash market to 1.2 zettabytes by 2030.

Memory and storage semiconductor equities surged to the top of the S&P 500 on Thursday, taking support from aggressive long-term growth guidance from SanDisk Corp.

SanDisk led the sector with a 15% surge, while Western Digital (WDC) gained 10%, SK Hynix (SKHY) climbed 8%, Micron Technology (MU) advanced 6%, and Super Micro (SMCI) rose 5% at the time of writing on Thursday.

SanDisk Investor Day Signals Structural Sector Shift

The catalyst for the broader semiconductor surge stemmed directly from SanDisk's 2026 Investor Day presentation, "SanDisk in Focus," during which executive leadership presented a multi-year financial framework that reset expectations across the memory ecosystem.

For fiscal years 2028 through 2030, SanDisk outlined targets for mid-to-high-teens compound revenue growth, supported by non-GAAP gross margins near 80%, operating margins near 75%, and adjusted free cash flow margins around 50%. The company also committed to returning all excess cash to shareholders following planned internal growth investments.

The bullish long-term framework directly benefited industry peers. Investors viewed SanDisk's pricing power and volume guarantees as evidence that memory economics are structurally improving, spilling over into higher valuations for Western Digital—which separated from SanDisk in 2025—as well as Micron (MU) and SK Hynix (SKHY).

SanDisk leadership attributed the expansion to booming enterprise demand, noting the data center flash market is projected to reach 1.2 zettabytes by 2030.

Recent Earnings Performance And Full-Year Outlook

Memory and server suppliers reported strong recent quarterly results despite brief market anxiety. SanDisk posted Q4 fiscal revenue of $8.97 billion, a 51% sequential surge led by data center flash demand, and projected Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue of $10.3 billion to $10.8 billion.

Western Digital closed fiscal 2026 with Q4 revenue up 44% year-over-year to $3.75 billion and non-GAAP EPS doubling to $3.56. Driven by data center expansion, it guided Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue to $4.1 billion.

title: Bernstein Makes Big Call on Super Micro Stock

Bernstein Makes Big Call on Super Micro Stock
Moz Farooque ACCA

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) is winning fresh Wall Street support after issuing unusually strong fiscal 2027 guidance, but Bernstein is stopping short of turning bullish. The firm raised its price target to $42 from $37 while maintaining a Market Perform rating, reflecting a growing tension for investors: explosive AI-server demand is improving Super Micro's outlook, but its execution record remains difficult to ignore.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 5 Warning Signs with SMCI.

Is SMCI fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

Super Micro builds servers, storage systems, networking equipment and liquid-cooled infrastructure used in AI, cloud and enterprise data centers. The company has become a major beneficiary of spending on GPU-heavy AI infrastructure, competing partly on its ability to rapidly integrate new processors into complete server systems.

Bernstein analyst Marc Newman highlighted Super Micro's fiscal 2027 revenue guidance of $65 billion to $72 billion, well above the $54.4 billion consensus cited in his note. For the September quarter, Super Micro expects $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion in revenue and adjusted EPS of $1.01 to $1.10.

The optimism follows a sharp improvement in profitability. Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue reached $11.1 billion, nearly doubling year over year, while non-GAAP gross margin surged to 17.6%. Super Micro also entered fiscal 2027 with record backlog after receiving more than $60 billion of new orders.

Still, Bernstein remains cautious. Newman noted Super Micro's poor history of revenue and earnings misses, saying, we give the company some benefit of the doubt.

That skepticism matters after SMCI jumped roughly 13% Wednesday following earnings. Shares were up about 23% for 2026 but remained below year-earlier levels.

Investor Takeaway

Super Micro now needs to prove its blockbuster guidance is executable.

Investors should focus on quarterly revenue conversion from the record backlog, gross margins and share dilution. The company's first-quarter margin guidance of 10.4% to 10.8%, cited by Bernstein, implies a sizable retreat from Q4's unusually strong 17.6%, making profitability a particularly important test.

Execution risk also extends beyond operations. Super Micro has disclosed an independent board review related to export-control issues, while its growing dependence on large customers could make results more volatile.

If Super Micro delivers against its $65 billion-plus revenue outlook while stabilizing margins, Bernstein's caution could eventually look conservative. Another string of misses, however, would reinforce why the firm stopped at Market Perform.

AI infrastructure companies have been having a ball this week. It started with a bang after bellwether Nvidia (NVDA) essentially turned its GPUs into an asset class with a $500 billion war chest and some of the leading asset managers of the world, including BlackRock (BLK), Blackstone (BLX), and KKR (KKR). Joining the party with Super Micro Computer (SMCI) and the neocloud company Nebius (NBIS) is the latter's competitor, CoreWeave (CRWV). The Mike Intrator-led necloud company's shares were down about 30% from its last earnings report. However, with the latest Q2 2026 numbers, CRWV stock rallied by 19.3% in yesterday's trading session.

About CoreWeave

Founded in 2017 as a cryptocurrency mining business, CoreWeave occupies the vaunted position of being one of the foremost AI infrastructure companies in the world. Now, CoreWeave provides enormous amounts of specialized computing power to companies developing and running AI. It operates data centers containing large clusters of Nvidia GPUs, with the overall objective of making thousands of GPUs behave like a single high-performance computing system. It is also concentrating on building a software stack, with its capabilities launching in 2026 to connect training, inference, observability, reinforcement learning, and autonomous agent improvement.

Revenue Doubles, Yet Losses Remain an Eyesore

In Q2 2026, CoreWeave's revenue stood at $2.6 billion. Not only did this mark a YoY growth of 116.7%, but it was also a beat on the Street's estimate. However, as one goes down the income statement, the picture gets a bit murkier despite all the optimism around backlog, capex, and revenue guidance.

Operating income margins slid to 5% from 16% in the year-ago period, while the company reported a net loss per share of $1.14 per share. Although this was lower than the consensus estimate of a loss of $1.47 per share, it almost doubled from the previous year's figure of a loss of $0.60 per share. Notably, this was the third consecutive quarter of losses widening for the company.

Because Lenovo competes directly with every name on this list, a beat of that magnitude signals genuine end-market demand across the group. Strength spanned AI infrastructure and PCs, which is why the move reaches HPQ as well as the server names. Lenovo trades in Hong Kong and is not a US-listed idea. Its 215% year to date move on the LNVGY ADR shows how the market is repricing this cycle.

Super Micro Extends Its Post-Earnings Run

The headline number for Wall Street was FY27 revenue guidance of $65 billion to $72 billion, versus Wall Street expectations of $53.3 billion.
